summary.text: For \(k\ge 60\), set \(n=2k+1\); if no two primes summed to \(4k+2=2n\), then every entry in the first row would vanish, since its potential prime pair is \((n-j,n+j)\), forcing the determinant to be zero. The cases \(1\le k<60\) are covered by explicit prime decompositions of \(4k+2\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(a(n)\) be the determinant of the \(n\times n\) integer matrix \(M_n\), whose rows and columns are indexed by \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\), and whose entries are
\[
 (M_n)_{i,j}=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Here the subtractions are natural-number subtractions. Since \(0\le i,j<n\), the expressions involved in the argument below have the ordinary integer values indicated; in particular, when \(i=0\) and \(0\le j<n\), we have \(n-j\ge 1\), so no truncation issue arises.

Assume the conjectured nonvanishing statement
\[
  n>120\text{ and }n\text{ odd}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a(n)\ne 0.
\]
We prove that for every positive integer \(k\), the integer \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

First dispose of the finite range \(1\le k<60\). The following table gives, for each such \(k\), primes \(p,q\) satisfying \(p+q=4k+2\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c@{\qquad}c|c@{\qquad}c|c}
 k&(p,q)&p+q&k&(p,q)&p+q\\ \hline
 1&(3,3)&6& 2&(3,7)&10\\
 3&(3,11)&14&4&(5,13)&18\\
 5&(3,19)&22&6&(3,23)&26\\
 7&(7,23)&30&8&(3,31)&34\\
 9&(7,31)&38&10&(5,37)&42\\
 11&(3,43)&46&12&(3,47)&50\\
 13&(7,47)&54&14&(5,53)&58\\
 15&(3,59)&62&16&(5,61)&66\\
 17&(3,67)&70&18&(3,71)&74\\
 19&(5,73)&78&20&(3,79)&82\\
 21&(3,83)&86&22&(7,83)&90\\
 23&(5,89)&94&24&(19,79)&98\\
 25&(5,97)&102&26&(3,103)&106\\
 27&(3,107)&110&28&(5,109)&114\\
 29&(5,113)&118&30&(13,109)&122\\
 31&(13,113)&126&32&(3,127)&130\\
 33&(3,131)&134&34&(7,131)&138\\
 35&(3,139)&142&36&(7,139)&146\\
 37&(11,139)&150&38&(3,151)&154\\
 39&(7,151)&158&40&(5,157)&162\\
 41&(3,163)&166&42&(3,167)&170\\
 43&(7,167)&174&44&(5,173)&178\\
 45&(3,179)&182&46&(5,181)&186\\
 47&(11,179)&190&48&(3,191)&194\\
 49&(5,193)&198&50&(3,199)&202\\
 51&(7,199)&206&52&(11,199)&210\\
 53&(3,211)&214&54&(7,211)&218\\
 55&(11,211)&222&56&(3,223)&226\\
 57&(3,227)&230&58&(5,229)&234\\
 59&(5,233)&238&&&
\end{array}
\]
The sums in the last column of each block are visibly \(4k+2\). Every number occurring as a component of one of these pairs is prime. This can be checked by trial division: for each number it suffices to test divisibility by primes not exceeding its square root (and the largest number here is \(233\), whose square root is less than \(16\), so only \(2,3,5,7,11,13\) can need testing). Thus the desired conclusion holds throughout \(1\le k<60\).

It remains to consider \(k\ge 60\). Set
\[
 n=2k+1.
\]
Then \(n\) is odd, and
\[
 n=2k+1\ge 121>120.
\]
The assumed nonvanishing conjecture therefore gives
\[
 a(n)=\det(M_n)\ne 0.
\]

We now show that this forces \(4k+2\) to be a sum of two primes. Consider the row of \(M_n\) indexed by \(i=0\). For a column index \(j\), where \(0\le j<n\), the two numbers tested for primality in this entry are
\[
 p_j=n+0-j=n-j
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 q_j=n+j-0=n+j.
\]
Because \(j<n\), \(p_j=n-j\) is a positive integer. Moreover,
\[
 p_j+q_j=(n-j)+(n+j)=2n=2(2k+1)=4k+2.
\]
Thus, if any entry in row \(0\) is \(1\), then by the definition of the matrix both \(p_j\) and \(q_j\) are prime, and the displayed equality supplies the required representation
\[
 4k+2=p_j+q_j.
\]

Suppose, for contradiction, that no such representation exists; that is, suppose there are no primes \(p,q\) with \(4k+2=p+q\). For every column \(j\), the pair \((p_j,q_j)=(n-j,n+j)\) sums to \(4k+2\). Consequently the two numbers \(p_j,q_j\) cannot both be prime. By the definition of \(M_n\), its \((0,j)\)-entry is therefore \(0\). Since this holds for every \(j=0,1,\ldots,n-1\), the entire row indexed by \(0\) is zero.

A square matrix with a zero row has determinant zero. Indeed, in the permutation expansion of the determinant, every product contains exactly one entry from that row, and that factor is zero. Hence \(\det(M_n)=0\), or equivalently \(a(n)=0\). This contradicts the nonvanishing already obtained from \(n>120\) and the oddness of \(n\).

Therefore a prime pair summing to \(4k+2\) must exist for every \(k\ge 60\). Together with the explicit finite table for \(1\le k<60\), this proves that for every integer \(k>0\) there are primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
 4k+2=p+q.
\]
Thus the conjectured nonvanishing of \(a(n)\) at every odd \(n>120\) implies Goldbach's conjecture for all even integers of the form \(4k+2\).
